title: Create your first ESP project
why: A saved project keeps the board, peripherals, wiring, Logics, and firmware settings together.
steps: Start a new configuration and give it a recognizable project filename.
Select the exact ESP board before adding hardware so pin validation uses the right constraints.
Add one peripheral, review the generated wiring, then save the project.
Compile only after validation reports no blocking issue.

title: Select an ESP board
why: The board determines chip family, flash layout, exposed pins, reserved pins, and available interfaces.
steps: Open Device Setup and choose the board matching the label and module on your hardware.
Compare the displayed pin layout with the physical board.
Review reserved and boot pins before accepting manual GPIO overrides.

title: Add peripherals
why: A peripheral profile supplies pin roles and capabilities used by wiring, Logics, and generated firmware.
steps: Open Peripherals and choose the hardware category.
Select the exact model when available; use Custom only when you can verify every signal.
Add another slot for each separate physical device.
Check required power rails and signal direction in the generated wiring.

title: Understand automatic GPIO assignment
why: Automatic assignment avoids many reserved-pin and interface conflicts while keeping a valid board-specific layout.
steps: Add the board and all intended peripherals first.
Inspect each assigned signal in GPIO configuration.
If you override a pin, verify voltage, direction, boot restrictions, and shared-bus rules.
Resolve every conflict before compilation.

title: Read the wiring diagram
why: The diagram converts logical signal names into concrete board pins and power connections.
steps: Match the selected board orientation to the physical board.
Trace each colored signal from the peripheral label to its GPIO.
Connect GND before signal testing and use only the documented supply voltage.
Re-open the diagram after any profile or GPIO change.

title: Create your first Logics automation
why: An automation needs a value or event, a decision when appropriate, and an execution path into an action.
steps: Add an On Start or sensor block.
Add a compatible action for a configured peripheral.
Connect typed value ports only to compatible inputs and white Flow ports to action inputs.
Group the complete automation and use Play, Pause, and Stop to control it.

title: Sensor → Compare → IF → Relay
why: The sensor supplies a number, Compare creates a Boolean, and IF converts the decision into an execution route.
steps: Connect Sensor Value to Compare A and set B to the threshold.
Connect Compare Result to IF Condition.
Provide a Flow trigger to IF In.
Connect IF True to Relay ON and IF False to Relay OFF.

title: Battery voltage warning
why: Rising Edge announces a threshold crossing once instead of repeating continuously while voltage stays low.
steps: Connect Battery Voltage to Compare A and set B to 11.8 V or the verified limit for your system.
Select the less-than operator.
Connect Result to Rising Edge Value.
Connect Rising Edge Out to MQTT Publish, display, or audio action.

title: MQTT live-value notification
why: A timer provides periodic Flow while the sensor value supplies the message payload.
steps: Configure and test the MQTT broker first.
Start a Timer from On Start or use its Enabled input and set the interval.
Connect Timer Out to MQTT Publish In.
Set an exact topic, enter optional text, and connect the sensor to Append value.
Choose Retained and QoS only according to the receiver’s needs.

title: OLED display output
why: A configured display action can show a live or composed value without writing display code.
steps: Add a supported display and confirm its bus and address.
Add its Set text action in Logics.
Connect Flow to In and a Text block or composed live value to Text.
Set display duration and compile the project.

title: Beep every 5 seconds above 50 °C
why: Compare supplies a live Boolean level; Timer turns that level into a repeated Flow pulse while the temperature remains above the threshold.
goal: Make the GPIO7 buzzer beep every five seconds while the ESP chip temperature is above 50 °C, then stop automatically when it falls to 50 °C or below.
prerequisites: Configure a passive two-wire Buzzer with SIG on GPIO7 and GND on board ground.
Open Logics and confirm Buzzer Play appears under Active peripherals.
Remember that chip temperature is the ESP die temperature, not room temperature.
steps: Add Hardware monitor · Chip temperature (°C) and connect its Value output to Compare A.
Set Compare B to 50 and Operator to >. Result is now True only while chip temperature is above 50 °C.
Add Timer, set Seconds to 5, and connect Compare Result to Timer Enabled. Do not use Rising Edge here: it emits only one Flow pulse when False becomes True.
Add the configured Buzzer Play action. Leave Source unconnected, choose the Beep preset and Passive mode, then connect Timer Out to Buzzer Play In.
Select all four blocks and group them. Select Start on that group. The Start control saves pending edits first and then changes the group state to Playing.
Use the Play button inside Buzzer Play to test the output directly. Use Stop to silence the test independently of the automation.
Confirm the wires animate while the group is running and Buzzer Play pulses every five seconds while Compare Result is True.
Select Stop on the group when testing is complete, then Save & apply and reboot once to verify the chosen state and graph persist.
explanation: Rising Edge is correct for a single over-temperature alarm: it fires once at the moment the value crosses above 50 °C. A recurring alarm needs Timer. Connecting Compare Result to Timer Enabled keeps the timer active only while the condition is True, and Timer Out supplies a new execution pulse every five seconds. Buzzer Play runs once for each incoming pulse.
verify: The Buzzer Play block’s direct Play button produces a beep on GPIO7.
When chip temperature is above 50 °C, Timer Out and the wire to Buzzer Play show recurring activity.
At 50 °C or below, the Timer is disabled and no recurring beep is produced.
After Save & apply and reboot, the graph, group, wiring, and selected runtime state are restored.

title: Audio and TTS notification
why: The source chain describes audio content while a separate Flow event starts playback.
steps: Configure a DAC or compatible audio output.
Connect Text to Offline TTS Text and TTS Speech to Audio Play Source.
Connect Rising Edge or another Flow event to Audio Play In.
Adjust speech rate, pitch, and intonation for clarity, then test on the target output.

title: Compile firmware
why: Compilation validates the selected target and embeds the current configuration and Logics graph.
steps: Save the project and resolve all validation errors.
Open Compile and Flash and choose the intended board target.
Start compilation and keep Technical Details available if a failure occurs.
Confirm the resulting manifest identifies the expected board and version.

title: Flash via USB
why: USB flashing installs the complete image and can apply reviewed configuration directly after verification.
steps: Connect a data-capable USB cable and close other serial tools.
Choose the correct device and start USB flash.
Review differences between the connected device and the project. Keep the device values, overwrite selected areas, or explicitly choose erase; erase is off by default.
Follow the boot-mode prompt if automatic reset cannot enter the loader.
Wait for write verification and configuration acknowledgement before disconnecting.

title: OTA update
why: OTA updates the application without opening the enclosure, but requires a reachable compatible device and sufficient OTA layout space.
steps: Keep the phone or PC on the same reachable network as the device.
Enter or discover the device address and verify identity.
Review differences between the connected device and the project. Keep the device values, overwrite selected areas, or explicitly choose erase; erase is off by default.
Compile for the detected chip and confirm the update prompt.
Wait for upload, reboot, and post-update reachability checks.

title: Use Serial Monitor
why: Serial logs reveal boot reasons, network status, peripheral initialization, and runtime errors.
steps: Connect the device by USB and close any program already using the port.
Open Serial Monitor and select the device.
Reset the board to capture boot output.
Copy only non-sensitive diagnostic lines when reporting a problem.

title: Compilation troubleshooting
why: The first failing validation or compiler message usually identifies the actionable cause.
steps: Expand Technical Details and find the first error, not only the final summary.
Verify board, peripheral profiles, and GPIO conflicts.
Retry after correcting the identified field.
Report the version, target board, and sanitized first error if the problem remains.

title: USB troubleshooting
why: USB failures commonly come from charge-only cables, busy ports, missing boot mode, or unstable power.
steps: Use a known data cable and direct USB port.
Close serial monitors and other flash tools.
Reconnect while following the displayed BOOT/RESET sequence.
Retry at a stable connection and review verification output.

title: OTA troubleshooting
why: Discovery and upload require network reachability in addition to firmware compatibility.
steps: Open the device address in a normal browser from the same phone or PC.
Check IP address, Wi-Fi isolation, VPN, firewall, and web credentials.
Verify the reported chip and ELMA firmware identity.
Use USB recovery if the device cannot accept a compatible OTA image.
